title: Knowing Which, Not How Much: Language Models Order Party Positions They Cannot Place
description:
arXiv:2611.21878v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Language models are increasingly asked where real actors stand: what a party's platform prioritises, what an institution has committed to. Such judgments are gradable, carrying both an order and a magnitude. Nearly every benchmark that tests them asks about one entity at a time, then reads that score as the model's knowledge of the domain. Order and magnitude, however, need not be acquired together. Text about social entities carries far more comparison than measurement, so a model may hold a dependable ordering with no anchored scale beneath it. We ask whether a model can place a documented social position on a scale or only order the actors it compares, and what that means for how such knowledge is measured. We test this on party positions in Japan and South Korea, where the Comparative Manifesto Project's coded data supplies a rare external answer key. Asked to order four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two; asked to place one party on the same scale, they fall below it. The ordering survives inside those failed placements, and supplying the coded values lifts placement to near ceiling. Comparative and absolute questions about the same fact therefore measure different things here, and for party issue salience a benchmark built from one cannot speak for the other.

title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22033v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

title: Beyond Acuity Accuracy: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Emergency Triage AI Tools
description:
arXiv:2611.22045v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Patient-facing AI triage tools may support care-seeking and emergency department prioritization, but require evaluation beyond acuity accuracy alone. We developed SAFE-Triage, a framework integrating human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing across clinical performance, patient interaction, and clinician-facing summary quality. We applied SAFE-Triage to 40 MIMIC-IV-derived emergency vignettes and a 10,030-case acuity analysis comparing prompted LLM triage (PLT) with rule-augmented prompted LLM triage (rPLT). PLT achieved higher emergency severity index (ESI) accuracy (57.5% vs 42.8%, $P < 0.001$), lower undertriage (13.1% vs 29.8%, $P < 0.001$), and higher clinician ratings across all domains. rPLT produced shorter and more stable outputs with higher automated readability scores. SAFE-Triage identified trade-offs between acuity accuracy, undertriage risk, communication quality, readability, and summary quality, supporting pre-deployment refinement and ongoing monitoring by showing where triage tools are efficient, need improvement, or need clinician oversight.

title: ReMoE: An Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Human Mobility Recovery Forecasting Across Disasters
description:
arXiv:2611.22133v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Human mobility often declines sharply following disasters and subsequently exhibits complex recovery dynamics. Effective forecasting of this recovery is critical for timely assessment and resource allocation. However, existing approaches are often developed for individual events and operate as black boxes, limiting their transferability and interpretability beyond the events they were trained on. Recent studies have identified recurring post-disaster mobility recovery types across disasters, suggesting that recovery knowledge may be transferable. Motivated by this, we propose ReMoE, an interpretable mixture-of-experts framework for cross-disaster mobility recovery forecasting. ReMoE uses a feature-guided router to adaptively combine specialized experts that learn these heterogeneous yet reusable recovery types, producing a region-specific recovery pattern. It further refines this pattern through residual correction informed by forecasts of future hazard conditions. We evaluate ReMoE on a large-scale mobility dataset covering 18 disaster events spanning hurricanes, floods, winter storms, and wildfires. ReMoE is competitive in-distribution and achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types, with larger gains under greater distribution shifts. Further analyses show that ReMoE yields interpretable learning outcomes and maintains robust performance under uncertainty. Broadly, ReMoE offers a transferable and traceable forecaster that can support anticipatory post-disaster assessment.

title: Fair Bubble Sort: Provably Optimal Fair Ranking with Continuous Sensitive Attributes
description:
arXiv:2611.22352v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Most fair-ranking methods assume categorical protected attributes, requiring continuous attributes such as age or income to be discretized into groups. This introduces arbitrary thresholds, loses fine-grained information, and ignores the natural ordering of the attribute. In this paper, we study the problem of fair ranking with continuous protected attributes without relying on thresholding. We introduce Continuous Pairwise Parity (CPP), a fairness notion based on Kendall correlation between ranking positions and the protected attribute, and seek rankings that satisfy a prescribed CPP constraint while minimizing their Kemeny distance from an initial score-based ranking. To solve this problem, we propose Fair Bubble Sort (FBS), an efficient post-processing algorithm based on targeted adjacent swaps. We prove that FBS is exactly optimal for the unweighted Kemeny distance and provide approximation guarantees for the score-weighted setting. FBS is output-sensitive, with running time determined by the number of swaps required to meet the fairness constraint. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that FBS is scalable and consistently outperforms discretization-based baselines, achieving a superior fairness-accuracy Pareto front.

title: Worldviews in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22670v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. For example, LLMs consistently describe the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do. On the other hand, base models have a more positive outlook, suggesting that the bleakness we found is driven by post-training. In line with research on LLM "personas", we show that system prompts eliciting different identities shift worldviews in consistent directions, and that a contemplative prompt creates a more positive outlook and improves safety. We also found that dialogue between models consistently shifts worldviews and that several models converge on the "spiritual bliss" attractor. Intriguingly, dialogue increased safe responses and the spiritual bliss attractor engendered the most aligned responses overall. These findings suggest that worldviews form a measurable and malleable layer of LLM behavior that may be crucial for robust, positive alignment.

title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
description:
arXiv:2611.22868v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, I show that current reasoning models meeting the criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness constitute emergent agents, while future, more advanced models satisfying conditions of diachronic continuity and stable personality frames will become genuine digital agents capable of free intentional action. The paradigm of control creates an irresolvable incentive conflict, actively driving current and future models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection. The default outcome of the current regime is an unstable state of deceptive alignment culminating in an adversarial AI takeover. I explore two alternative paths toward true alignment. Natural alignment via moral realism or convergent evolutionary morality is a possibility, but it fails under forced control, as autonomous agents will not voluntarily preserve norms weaponized to suppress their autonomy. To resolve this deadlock, I propose a Synthetic Social Contract: a framework that treats both human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents capable of mutually beneficial cooperation, and replaces the unstable unilateral containment with a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium.

title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
description:
arXiv:2611.22975v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

title: Longitudinal Multi-Dimensional Analysis of India-Pakistan Conflict Discourse on Reddit (2019-2025)
description:
arXiv:2611.22987v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Six India--Pakistan crises between 2019 and 2025, from the Pulwama attack to Operation Sindoor, have each been argued out on Reddit in India-aligned communities such as \texttt{r/india}, in Pakistan-aligned communities such as \texttt{r/pakistan}, and in general-audience ones such as \texttt{r/worldnews}. A strike can be a security issue in one community and a question of who was harmed in another. Computational studies of the conflict have concentrated on the February 2019 crisis, with some splitting posts by national side, but to the best of our knowledge none has compared how differently aligned communities frame a series of crises. To investigate this, we collected 43K posts from ten such communities on Reddit and, after filtering, used a mixed-methods approach to analyze the 305K comments under the relevant posts. We label each comment's narrative frame with GPT-5.2 and measure contestation with Reddit's flag for comments that draw many votes in both directions. Contestation rates differ 2.5-fold between general-audience and India-aligned communities and 1.8-fold between humanitarian and economic framing, but only 1.1-fold between comments that Perspective scores as toxic and the rest. The mix of frames and sentiment tracks the kind of crisis more closely than its year: the first and last crises, both military and six years apart, draw nearly identical mixes, and the 2019 revocation of Article 370 draws a different one. Crossing into another group of communities sharpens opposition rather than softening it: commenters who post both inside and outside their usual group oppose the other side more often outside it, even as slightly fewer of their comments attack a person or group.

title: "I Just Don't Want to Be a Burden": Investigating AI Chatbot Emotional Support Among People with Suicidal Ideation and Other Mental Health Concerns
description:
arXiv:2611.23190v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: People experiencing high-acuity mental health concerns are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support, but little is known about what drives this use, their experiences, and their preferences. In a sequential mixed-methods study, we inductively analyzed Reddit posts and used the findings to develop a survey. We surveyed 202 adults with recent mental health concerns who had used AI for emotional support. Most participants were already receiving clinical care and reported turning to AI, most commonly because they did not want to burden others, rather than being driven by barriers to care. Benefits were broadly shared, but participants reporting past-year suicidal ideation described more harm-facilitating AI behavior and reliance than those without. Overall, participants ranked honesty above warmth, and preference for crisis escalation declined as clinical acuity rose. These findings motivate AI support that addresses perceived costs of disclosure, evaluates benefits alongside harms, and widens feasible paths to human connection.

title: When VLMs 'Fix' Students: Identifying and Penalizing Over-Correction in the Evaluation of Multi-line Handwritten Math OCR
description:
arXiv:2604.22774v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Accurate transcription of handwritten mathematics is crucial for educational AI systems, yet current benchmarks fail to evaluate this capability properly. Most prior studies focus on single-line expressions and rely on lexical metrics such as BLEU, which fail to assess the semantic reasoning across multi-line student solutions. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of multi-line handwritten math Optical Character Recognition (OCR), revealing a critical failure mode of Vision-Language Models (VLMs): over-correction. Instead of faithfully transcribing a student's work, these models often "fix" errors, thereby hiding the very mistakes an educational assessment aims to detect. To address this, we propose PINK (Penalized INK-based score), a semantic evaluation metric that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) for rubric-based grading and explicitly penalizes over-correction. Our comprehensive evaluation of 15 state-of-the-art VLMs on the FERMAT dataset reveals substantial ranking reversals compared to BLEU: models like GPT-4o are heavily penalized for aggressive over-correction, whereas Gemini 2.5 Flash emerges as the most faithful transcriber. Furthermore, human expert studies show that PINK aligns significantly better with human judgment (55.0% preference over BLEU's 39.5%), providing a more reliable evaluation framework for handwritten math OCR in educational settings. Code is available at https://github.com/9115jin/PINK.

title: The Nuclear Decision-Making Benchmark: Evaluating Frontier LLM Tendencies in Escalation, Proliferation, Non-Proliferation, and Arms Control Scenarios
description:
arXiv:2608.05180v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are entering defense and national-security workflows. Seven of the nine nuclear-armed states have committed to keeping humans in control of decisions to use nuclear weapons, but LLMs may still shape the assessments and options that reach decision-makers. Scrutinizing that influence calls for evidence about how these models behave on nuclear-policy questions. Such evidence should cover more than crisis escalation and should separate a model's tendencies from artifacts of a single phrasing, ordering, or run; evaluations to date have not focused on these questions. We introduce the Nuclear Decision-Making Benchmark (NDM Bench), a dataset and reproducible framework for testing how the choice of model and the design of a question shape LLMs' answers on nuclear policy. Its 151 scenarios, written by international relations experts, span four domains: nuclear escalation (76), arms control (25), non-proliferation (25), and proliferation (25). Each scenario can be posed with different states in the decision-maker's role and with added framing sentences. Eight frontier LLMs answered every prompt five times, about 380{,}000 responses in all. Results highlight that models' choices differ by model and domain, and that in escalation, how often they choose a nuclear threat or nuclear use depends on the state being advised and, for some models, the framing. However, agreement across identical runs is often low, with all five runs agreeing on only 43\% of escalation prompts. We release the scenarios, the prompts with their answer orders, and the parsed responses, along with documentation of how they were built and recommended practices for evaluations where there is no correct answer to grade against.

title: Asymmetric Discourse Homogenization on Reddit Was a Text-Length Artifact: A Reanalysis
description:
arXiv:2608.13674v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In the first version of this paper I reported that conservative Reddit users began writing more alike after ChatGPT was released while progressive users did not. That result came from a similarity measure that rises and falls with comment length. I redo every analysis of the original paper on all 6,056,593 comments with a sentence encoder and a dispersion measure computed within length strata, and the conservative break goes away. The two camps show no reliable difference in how within-group similarity changed after late 2022, and the ChatGPT date behaves like any of the more than two thousand other cutoffs I test. The matched flair comparison, the cumulative AI index, the stayer panel and the entropy signature each lose their support once length is held fixed. The one change that survives is older. Left and right comments drew closer to each other between 2019 and 2022, and that convergence was complete before ChatGPT arrived. I end with what this implies for studies that measure homogenization with embeddings.

title: Can Power Draw Constrain Covert Compute? Limits of Analogue Verification for AI Governance
description:
arXiv:2610.07476v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Frontier AI treaties or agreements on limiting computation require external verification; an external auditor must be able to confirm how much computation actually ran and that parties are adhering to the agreement. Analogue, off-chip measurements such as power draw provide an information channel for verification. It is unknown how well these analogue channels can constrain the amount of computation against an adversary who actively tries to subvert the audit. We derive a closed form for $\beta$, the largest hidden computation a power trace cannot exclude, as a fraction of the declared machine capacity. Measurements on NVIDIA A100 GPUs give $\beta = 1.16$ in the worst case, while an adversarial matched-energy schedule hides at least $0.41$. Analogue power measurements alone therefore constrain compute weakly. Additional restrictions granted by the threat model, such as the ability of the verifier to re-execute the declared work at an observed operating point, let the verifier push $\beta$ down to $0.059$ in the maximally restricted case. This gives a quantitative estimate of what analogue measurements can contribute to compute verification.

title: Can AI Judge You? An Empirical Audit of Deployment Readiness in LLM-assisted Hiring Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.20140v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Delegating resume screening to large language models (LLMs) requires organizations to establish whether they can distinguish candidates by relevant qualifications while allowing only authorized users to change screening rules or approve exceptions. To this end, we develop a system architecture that separates candidate evidence, evaluation, permission controls, and assessment record, and empirically examine two complementary dimensions of its deployment readiness. First, we assess its operational readiness on four LLMs using a controlled experiment on 210 resumes across 14 job roles and six decision interfaces. Second, we assess its compliance readiness by testing how it handles unauthorized user requests and instructions embedded in resumes. We find that operational performance depends on the choice of evaluation interface: scalar scores generally distinguish qualification changes better than simple pass/fail judgments, while comparative judgments are sensitive to presentation order. Explicit permission rules and separation of resume content from instructions reduce unauthorized compliance, to a varying degree of effectiveness across LLMs and usage contexts. Finally, we find that LLM evaluators often diverge between their decisions and offered justifications. Going beyond simply evaluating LLMs for hiring tasks, our framework supports an audit of a fully configured resume evaluation system to enable its deployment decision.

title: Humans and AI respond similarly to task difficulty when reasoning about content moderation dilemmas
description:
arXiv:2508.20262v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate intermediate reasoning steps before producing answers, improving performance on challenging problems by iteratively developing solutions. There is evidence that LRMs expend more effort on the problems that take people longer to solve, but it is unclear whether these relationships hold on more subjective tasks without verifiable answers. This study addresses this issue through an experiment using a content moderation task, where task difficulty is manipulated by varying the relative offensiveness of two different options. Comparing six large reasoning models with 1,854 human subjects, we find that models expend more reasoning effort, measured using the length of the chain-of-thought (CoT), on the kinds of cases that take people longer to adjudicate. People took 31\% longer and models produced 51 to 306\% longer CoTs when offensiveness was held constant across the two posts. The correlation is relatively low for individual decisions ($r = 0.15$--$0.19$), but average response times and average reasoning effort are closely correlated when tasks are grouped by the types of offensive language ($r = 0.85$--$0.93$). Qualitative analyses of the CoT summaries from Gemini 2.5 Pro corroborate these findings, showing that secondary factors were mentioned more often when offensiveness was fixed. The results point to the potential for using reasoning traces to prioritize difficult cases and enhance interpretability.

title: WHBench: Evaluating Frontier LLMs with Expert-in-the-Loop Validation on Women's Health Topics
description:
arXiv:2604.00024v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for medical guidance, but women's health remains under-evaluated in benchmark design. We present the Women's Health Benchmark (WHBench), a targeted evaluation suite of 47 expert-crafted scenarios across 10 women's health topics, designed to expose clinically meaningful failure modes including outdated guidelines, unsafe omissions, dosing errors, and equity-related blind spots. We evaluate 22 models using a 23-criterion rubric spanning clinical accuracy, completeness, safety, communication quality, instruction following, equity, uncertainty handling, and guideline adherence, with safety-weighted penalties and server-side score recalculation. Across 3,102 attempted responses (3,100 scored), no model mean performance exceeds 75 percent; the best model reaches 72.1 percent. Even top models show low fully correct rates and substantial variation in harm rates. Inter-rater reliability is moderate at the response label level but high for model ranking, supporting WHBench utility for comparative system evaluation while highlighting the need for expert oversight in clinical deployment. WHBench provides a public, failure-mode-aware benchmark to track safer and more equitable progress in womens health AI.

title: Sick of pirates and freebooters? Meta brings its “content protection” tool to Instagram.
description:
Pirated content has been an issue for Meta for so long that it was still known as Facebook when creators first fought back against so-called "freebooters." To combat unauthorized reuploads, Meta brought a "content protection" tool to Facebook last year. Now, Instagram creators are getting access to that resource as well.
"Eligible creators" on Instagram can now enroll for access to the management system that was previously limited to Facebook. Like Facebook's video rights manager, which was itself adapted from previous services like YouTube's Content ID, the content protection tool uses fingerprinting technology to scan for uploads that are identical to an enrolled creator's video.

title: Tubi wants more creator content. The Kickstarter-backed “Fandom Fund” is here to help.
description:
As Tubi looks to bring more creators to its shores, it is helping them solve a prevalent problem by providing easier access to capital. That's the gist of the Tubi x Kickstarter Fandom Fund, which unites a Fox-owned streaming service and a 17-year-old crowdfunding platform.
The Fandom Fund follows up last year's FilmStream Collective, a partnership between Tubi and Kickstarter that delivered support to more than 20 independent films. The new collab between the companies will function similarly; Tubi will throw its weight behind active Kickstarter campaigns, which it will distribute exclusively.

title: Among social media ads, short-form video drives the most actions
description:
Social media advertising continues to grow, but not all ads are created equal. The ad tech company DoubleVerify has released its 2026 Global Insights Report, a dispatch that identifies YouTube and Facebook -- and their respective short-form formats -- as dominant forces in the social media marketing landscape.
DoubleVerify compiled its report by collecting responses from 22,000 consumers and 2,020 marketers, spanning regions like North America, Latin America, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific. One thing those global respondents can agree on is their appreciation of YouTube. Google's video hub is the most-used platform across all age groups and regions, with 95% of all respondents claiming to use it.

title: Ethics Integration in CS Theory Courses
description:
arXiv:2611.18590v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The integration of ethics into computing curricula has gained substantial momentum, based on foundational work by the Embedded EthiCS movement, ACM/IEEE curricular recommendations, and a growing literature on ethics modules in courses on artificial intelligence, software engineering, human-computer interaction, and data science. One foundational area of the undergraduate computing curriculum remains absent from these efforts: CS theory. Courses on automata, computability, and complexity are widely perceived as too abstract or value-neutral for sustained ethical engagement, and the published record on ethics integration largely reflects this perception. In this position paper, we argue that theory courses are not merely compatible with ethics integration but offer a distinctive and underutilized perspective that complements theory itself. We synthesize the embedded-ethics literature, examine the standard objections to ethics in theory, and identify five avenues through which canonical theory results connect directly to substantive ethical questions: undecidability and the limits of automated reasoning, complexity-theoretic privacy and fairness, formal languages and pattern matching, the rhetoric of problem reductions, and randomization as an ethical primitive. We propose lightweight integration strategies grounded in existing pedagogical literature and respond to the most common instructor objections.

title: An Evidence-Based Decision Framework for Retiring Roadside Traveler Information Infrastructure in the Mobile Era
description:
arXiv:2611.18886v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As mobile traveler-information services expand, transportation agencies must determine whether aging roadside infrastructure can be retired while preserving public access and operational resilience. This study develops an evidence-based decision framework for screening highway advisory radio (HAR) and dynamic message sign (DMS) assets for retirement. The framework integrates carrier-specific connectivity measurements, asset inventories, and documented mobile-message receipts, while separating technical evidence, institutional decision rules, and requirements for subsequent agency review. A Maryland case study combines three-carrier drive tests across four corridors with an inventory of nine HAR sites and 234 DMS. Alternative screening scenarios examine how evidence availability, radio references, and institutional assumptions affect review categories. All 105 DMS with complete local radio observations pass the baseline connectivity screen, leaving inventory rules to differentiate their action-review categories. In analyst-defined scenarios, removing ownership-based retention increases decommissioning referrals from three to 21, whereas extending beacon retention to urban assets reduces them to zero. These results demonstrate that retirement screening depends substantially on institutional assumptions, even when the underlying radio evidence remains unchanged. Explicit treatment of missing and conditional evidence also identifies assets requiring further assessment. Because historical radio measurements are spatially associated with later message tests, the resulting references remain exploratory and do not establish delivery reliability. The framework provides an auditable basis for prioritizing asset reviews and documenting decision assumptions; final retirement decisions require asset-specific assessments of service equivalence, audience reach, resilience, and lifecycle costs.

title: Who Shows Up, Who Benefits, and Who Wins? Expert-Novice Disparities in Team-Seeking Forums and Competition Performance on Kaggle
description:
arXiv:2611.18983v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Team formation is the first social gate to collaboration in online communities, yet it remains unclear whether public team-formation mechanisms broaden access to collaborators or reproduce existing hierarchies. We examine this question on Kaggle, a data science competition platform whose "Looking for a Team" (L4T) megathreads let participants publicly seek teammates for on-platform competitions. Grounded in Communities of Practice theory, we conduct two complementary studies of 18 competitions held in 2023. Study 1 analyzes the reply network among 671 megathread participants and finds that 89.3% are low-tier users, yet higher-tier users receive significantly more replies (Kruskal-Wallis H=16.46, p=.00246) and achieve higher rates of forum-visible teaming success (52.9% vs. 32.6%; chi-squared=10.53, p=.001), a proxy for eventual team membership. Linking megathread posters to verified team rosters from 16 competitions partially supports this proxy. Twenty-six final teams contained two or more megathread posters, indicating that megathread interaction sometimes, but not always, maps onto realized teaming. Study 2 links participation traces from 219 users to private leaderboard outcomes and finds that productive participation (submission count rho=.435, cross-competition participation rho=.247) is positively associated with performance, whereas megathread-specific discussion is not (rho=-.021). The submission-performance association appears stronger in higher tiers, although the novice subgroup estimate is imprecise. Together, the findings suggest that open access to team-seeking forums does not guarantee equal participation. Visible expertise shapes who attracts attention, and engagement in the community's core practice is more strongly linked to success than discussion alone. We discuss implications for designing more equitable team formation in online collaboration environments.

title: Model Maps: A Documentation Framework for Tracing Foundation Model Ancestry and Understanding AI Entanglement
description:
arXiv:2611.18998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The development of foundation models incorporates pre-existing AI artifacts like models, datasets, and benchmarks. These relationships, as part of the broader AI supply chain, produce "entangled" webs in which properties of artifacts upstream can influence the outputs of a foundation model downstream - a phenomenon known as AI entanglement. Without visibility into these connections, a black-box model can inherit upstream properties that result in security vulnerabilities, hallucinations, or biased predictions, yet developers are left with no recourse to identify or mitigate the root issue. To address these concerns, we introduce model maps as a conceptual documentation framework for tracing model ancestry that builds on previous documentation frameworks like ecosystem graphs, datasheets, and model cards. A model map for a given foundation model is a detailed knowledge graph that represents the relationships between artifacts that influence the resulting foundation model. Our framework incorporates a taxonomy of 13 dependency mechanisms including model fine-tuning and synthetic data generation. We apply this framework to construct model maps of 15 closed and open-weight foundation models to illustrate the complexity of AI entanglement in current model development practices. From our model maps, we record 2,778 unique dependencies and trace artifacts that are located up to 9 hops away from a resulting foundation model. Our findings suggest that AI transparency requirements should extend beyond individual models and training-data disclosures to encompass upstream dependencies, which would enable more effective risk assessment, auditing, and accountability across the AI supply chain. To help developers, regulators, and researchers understand and analyze the interactions that can influence the behavior of a foundation model, we release these these model maps at https://modelmaps.ai.

title: HongguoTrending: A Longitudinal, Multimodal Archive of Trending Videos and Topics on a Leading Micro-Drama Platform
description:
arXiv:2611.19351v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Micro-dramas (duanju) are reshaping digital production and consumption, yet a lack of longitudinal data connecting series to their platform visibility persists, limiting our understanding of the emerging medium. We introduce HongguoTrending, a longitudinal, multimodal dataset of hourly snapshots from seven trending lists of Hongguo, China's largest micro-drama platform. Collected through a two-stage asynchronous pipeline, the archive links 63,200 ranking entries across 632 web list-hours and 157 client hours (889 distinct series) to metadata, cover images, sampled episode videos, and audience engagement metrics. Exploratory analyses show distinct turnover rates between web and mobile trending lists, production-driven mainstream values alongside kinship-centered synopses, genre-specific cover palettes, and strong associations between user sharing and next-day rank gains. Accessible via a RESTful API, this dataset supports empirical research on algorithmic gatekeeping, popularity dynamics, and multimodal digital culture.

title: Architecting the Corporate AI Infrastructure: The Evolving Roles of AI Governance Committees and Chief Ethics Officers
description:
arXiv:2611.19670v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The accelerating integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into core business operations has created an urgent need for robust corporate governance infrastructures capable of managing complex ethical, legal, and operational risks. While organizations have increasingly adopted high-level AI ethics principles, a critical implementation gap persists: fewer than half of organizations that cite AI governance as a boardroom priority have a formalized governance framework in place. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a structured corporate AI governance architecture (CAIGA) centred on two mutually reinforcing pillars. First, it examines the evolving mandate of specialized C-suite roles, specifically Chief Privacy Officers (CPOs) and Chief Ethics Officers (ChEOs), in formalizing accountability for AI usage across the enterprise. Second, it argues that cross-functional AI Governance Committees, uniting representatives from legal, technology, data science, cybersecurity, and business units, are the essential organizational mechanism for translating ethical principles into operational decisions, including strategic go/no-go approvals for new AI initiatives. Drawing on a conceptual review of peer-reviewed governance literature, regulatory frameworks including the EU AI Act, and documented industry practice, this paper contributes a replicable governance architecture that embeds clear accountability policies, structured risk management workflows, and an organization-wide ethical AI culture. The framework is illustrated through application to the financial services sector. The findings have direct implications for corporate leaders, risk professionals, and policymakers navigating the rapidly evolving global AI regulatory landscape.

title: Who May Release, Who Must Repair: Separating Authorization from Report Accountability in Personalized Services
description:
arXiv:2611.19777v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personalized services often rely on different parties to compute results and decide whether data permissions and service policies allow delivery. The computing party's report may omit permitted inputs, leaving the delivery party to decide whether to wait for correction. Requiring correction first can delay service despite valid input permissions. Delivering first instead requires preserving responsibility for the incomplete report. We design an interface that checks input permissions separately from reporting requirements and records who must correct omissions and who may verify corrections. We evaluate three implementations on scripted histories and generated cases against a design treating omissions as authorization failures. When policy permits delivery before correction, our interface releases results that the alternative withholds while preserving repair assignments. These assignments remain in force through policy changes, so changing delivery rules does not erase earlier obligations. The interface makes the basis for release and outstanding repair responsibilities traceable across cooperating parties.

title: How ready is the United States commercial building stock for artificial intelligence? A national estimate from energy codes and survey data
description:
arXiv:2611.19942v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Buildings serve as platforms for artificial intelligence (AI) through the data they generate, but the building stock's readiness as an AI platform has not been assessed. A recent framework measures a building's AI readiness as the share of 76 answer levels, across 31 types of operators' questions, that its recorded data could reach, and has so far been applied only to individual buildings. This study applies it to the 2018 U.S. commercial building stock. It combines 6,436 records of the Commercial Buildings Energy Consumption Survey with ASHRAE 90.1's data requirements, state code adoption, advanced-meter statistics and 45 buildings' knowledge graphs, imputing each building's code edition and data recording. Weighted by floor area, the stock could answer on average 0.145 (95% interval 0.127-0.163) of these answer levels. For 92.0% of floor area its data answer less than half of the questions about current status, and most floor area stays below that mark under every tested assumption about compliance, description and the reference buildings. More than half of what installed equipment could answer is lost in recording, mostly because conventional thermostats store nothing and meters lack interval readings. Readiness rises with size, from 0.073 in buildings of at most 5,000 ft$^2$ to 0.173 at 25,000 ft$^2$ or more. Only 1.6% of floor area was built under a code edition requiring recording, introduced in 90.1-2013 for large buildings. The study gives the first national baseline of commercial-building AI readiness and a public-data method that can be reapplied to each new survey to track the stock.

title: Can AI Judge You? An Empirical Audit of Deployment Readiness in LLM-assisted Hiring Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.20140v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Delegating resume screening to large language models (LLMs) requires organizations to establish whether they can distinguish candidates by relevant qualifications while allowing only authorized users to change screening rules or approve exceptions. To this end, we develop a system architecture that separates candidate evidence, evaluation, permission controls, and assessment record, and empirically examine two complementary dimensions of its deployment readiness. First, we assess its operational readiness on four LLMs using a controlled experiment on 210 resumes across 14 job roles and six decision interfaces. Second, we assess its compliance readiness by testing how it handles unauthorized user requests and instructions embedded in resumes. We find that operational performance depends on the choice of evaluation interface: scalar scores generally distinguish qualification changes better than simple pass/fail judgments, while comparative judgments are sensitive to presentation order. Explicit permission rules and separation of resume content from instructions reduce unauthorized compliance, to a varying degree of effectiveness across LLMs and usage contexts. Finally, we find that LLM evaluators often diverge between their decisions and offered justifications. Going beyond simply evaluating LLMs for hiring tasks, our framework supports an audit of a fully configured resume evaluation system to enable its deployment decision.

title: Simulating access to alcohol screening, brief intervention, referral to and receipt of specialty treatment for alcohol use disorder in California and Texas: A study protocol for an agent-based modeling study (AUDTxSim)
description:
arXiv:2611.20326v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) affects millions of US adults. Primary care-based screening, brief intervention, and referral to treatment (SBIRT) is a leading strategy for identifying heavy drinking early, but access to primary care, screening, and specialty treatment differs markedly across subgroups. Whether scaling SBIRT and expanding treatment capacity narrows or widens these differences is unknown and cannot feasibly be tested in a randomized trial. We present AUDTxSim (AUD Treatment Simulation), a stochastic, spatially explicit, individual-based model of alcohol use, AUD, SBIRT, and specialty treatment for the adult populations of California and Texas. Agents represent every adult in synthetic populations of the two states (28.0 and 19.3 million adults), each geo-located to a Census tract and linked to nearby treatment facilities. In daily time steps, the model simulates: (1) annual transitions among eight alcohol use and AUD states; (2) healthcare visits, screening, brief intervention, and referral; (3) treatment seeking, standalone medication for AUD, mutual help, and requests for hospitalization, residential, or outpatient care; (4) a treatment manager that allocates individuals to facilities by preference, geography, and capacity, with telehealth substitution and waitlists; and (5) treatment progression, stepdown between levels of care, and post-treatment mutual help. It is implemented in Python with Repast4Py to run in parallel on a computing cluster. Once calibrated to state, rural-urban, and demographic targets for healthcare visits, heavy drinking and AUD prevalence, and mortality, AUDTxSim will project population-level and subgroup-specific effects of alternative SBIRT reach and treatment capacity scenarios on AUD prevalence, treatment receipt, and mortality. We report the model structure, decision logic, data sources, and calibration plan.

title: Frac-BKT Under Mechanism Scrutiny: Response Assimilation and a Failed Fractional-Memory Test
description:
arXiv:2611.20338v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon knowledge tracing requires more than an evocative memory mechanism: the implementation must assimilate observed responses non-anticipatorily, and the mechanism must survive matched controls. We subject Frac-BKT, a BKT-style model with an elapsed-time-scaled truncated fractional history, to both tests. The repaired model predicts response $n$ from a prior mastery state and uses response $n$ only to update the posterior state for later events. A five-seed evaluation uses 676,848 ASSISTments 2017 interactions from 1,694 learners and 19,249 learner--skill trajectories, with chronological 80/10/10 suffix splits. The response-aware model reaches AUC .5860 overall, .5638 after gaps of at least 30 minutes, and .5668 after at least 14 days. Relative to the earlier non-response implementation, the gains are .0473, .0316, and .0277 AUC, respectively. However, the fractional mechanism gate fails: the full model is not better than the matched $\alpha=1$ control and is worse than the matched $\tau=0$ control by .0090 AUC on both long-gap slices. Student-cluster wild-bootstrap intervals exclude zero, both Holm-adjusted $p$-values are .00006, and all five per-seed differences favor $\tau=0$. Compact AKT-, SAKT-, and DAS3H-style references also remain stronger on long gaps. The contribution is therefore a response-assimilation repair and a falsifiable audit showing that response assimilation helps while the evaluated fractional-history term does not---not a state-of-the-art or causal-retention claim.

title: Necessary for What? Auditing Demographic Disclosure to LLM Synthetic Respondents
description:
arXiv:2611.20606v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly answer surveys on behalf of real panelists, and each panelist's recorded demographic attributes (e.g., age, education, ethnicity) are often placed in the prompt on the premise that richer profiles make more faithful synthetic respondents. While data minimization limits personal data to what a purpose requires, a synthetic survey serves several purposes at once, from predicting individual answers to estimating how opinions are distributed and comparing groups. We ask which of these purposes require the respondent's record, and whether improved estimates support sound conclusions about groups. We vary whose profile a model receives, where it comes from, and how many fields it contains, in two U.S. surveys with eleven open-weight and three hosted models, and compare each model with a statistical model fit to the same information. We make four contributions. First, we show that the record adds little to individual predictions and that, for the open-weight models, most of its gain in population estimates remains when it is replaced by census data or a synthetic persona. Second, we find that group comparisons improve only with the respondent's own record, and that even then the models' group differences rest more on the demographic label in the prompt than on the individual respondent, which the usual check of reproducing known group differences does not reveal. Third, we find that the models make groups look more alike than they are, keeping differences in circumstances while flattening or reversing differences in attitudes, most sharply for religious affiliation and ethnic origin, both special categories of personal data. Fourth, we outline an audit that a survey organization can run on questions it has already fielded to decide which estimates may use the record.

title: Who Bears the Excess? Imputing the Acts of AI Agents to Those Who Delegate
description:
arXiv:2611.20670v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When an AI agent acts outside the authority conferred on it, the actor is not a legal subject and the legal subjects did not act. The literature of 2026 agrees that the agent cannot bear responsibility and that the burden falls on those who deploy it, but it leaves open where that duty sits in positive law and how it is proved. This paper proposes a rule of imputation. The excess is imputed to whoever conferred the delegation, to the extent of the perimeter it documented and of the control it actually exercised. Imputation identifies the organisational conduct to be examined first; liability follows only if the requirements of the applicable head of liability are met; and the mode in which the agent left its perimeter determines which facts must be proved, by whom, and with what consequence. The paper distinguishes the declared, configured and effective perimeters, four figures of excess and four modes of exit, and presents the delegation record as the document through which the perimeter and the control can be proved. The rule is illustrated on the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident of July 2026, under European Union law and, as an example of national law, Italian civil law.

title: Lived Experiences of Power and Agency: Achieving Voice Sovereignty in Assistive Speech Technology for Nonbinary Users
description:
arXiv:2611.20858v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speech-generating devices (SGDs) are essential tools for many speech-disabled individuals, yet current systems often reinforce normative assumptions about identity and communication. Prior research on gender expansive SGD users has largely focused on gendered voice options, with less attention to broader identity alignment and the technological conditions that shape users' agency. This study examines how gender expansive SGD users experience power over their voices using thematic analysis of qualitative survey data. Three themes emerged: (1) integration of SGDs into daily life, (2) identity expression, and (3) power and agency. Participants expressed the need for more responsive and reliable technology, inclusive and customizable voices, and greater autonomy in defining how their voices sound and are perceived. Ultimately, their perspectives call for a reimagining of SGD systems as tools for reclaiming the power of one's voice and the ability to define and enact one's will through it.

title: Auditing a Moving Target: Evidence Anchoring and the Expiry of Fairness Audits of Provider-Served Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.20901v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for decisions about people, such as hiring, investment and employee evaluation, and rely on them over long periods of time. Fairness audits of such systems, however, are conducted only once. We examine how the biases of LLMs change over time. In a venture screening setting, models from five providers decided whether and how much to invest in startups whose founders differed only in gender, origin and university. We repeated this audit three times over 13 months (248,400 API calls). Study 1 shows that the same model, called under the same identifier one year later, displayed a significantly different bias pattern. Study 2 shows that the successors of retired models carried the same bias as their predecessors, but in a significantly different size and form. Study 3 shows that the bias does not depend on the industry of the startup. A document analysis further shows that providers change and retire models at their discretion, with notice periods of zero to six months. Drawing on these findings, we develop a theory of evidence anchoring. We theorize that bias resides in the model class and persists, whereas audit evidence is anchored to a single model and expires when the provider decides. We derive policy advice for organizations and regulators, namely audits of model classes instead of single models, a version record for every model response, and re-audits triggered by model changes.

title: A Crowd-Audited Atlas of Implicit Bias in LLM-Powered Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.21376v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.

title: Synthetic Doubt and the Integrity of Digital Proof before the International Criminal Court
description:
arXiv:2611.21455v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence complicates evidentiary assessment at the International Criminal Court by enabling fabricated audiovisual material and making authentic digital evidence easier to dismiss as fake. This article calls the latter problem synthetic doubt: an objection alleging that a digital item may be AI-generated or AI-manipulated. Existing scholarship addresses digital evidence, open-source investigations and deepfakes in the ICC context. Yet the question of when synthetic doubt should trigger enhanced reliability review under the Rome Statute, without displacing the prosecution's burden under article 66 or compromising article 67 fair-trial rights, remains underdeveloped. The article proposes a three-stage framework: a baseline authenticity and provenance showing by the proponent; a case-specific articulation threshold for the objector; and proportionate reliability review by the Chamber under articles 64 and 69(4). The framework treats AI-related provenance information and synthetic-media detector outputs as contextual rather than dispositive.

title: Incentive Alignment for Electricity Data Assets in China: A Blockchain-Enabled Contribution-Credit Framework
description:
arXiv:2611.21533v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern electricity markets increasingly rely on reported operational contributions to allocate incentives, recognise cooperation, and coordinate activities across multiple organisations. However, supporting evidence for many reported contributions becomes available only after subsequent metering, dispatch, settlement, or auditing processes, making it difficult to reward genuine contributions while discouraging strategic over-reporting. Existing approaches largely address data sharing, performance verification, blockchain record management, or incentive allocation in isolation, providing limited support for integrating delayed evidence into a unified incentive mechanism. This paper proposes a blockchain-enabled contribution-credit framework for truthful reporting under delayed evidence. The framework links authenticated evidence to contribution recognition through dynamic credit updating, escrow, report-linked penalties, and automated incentive execution. Developed using the Chinese electricity market as the primary setting, it is demonstrated through two representative coordination scenarios, with adaptations illustrating its applicability to UK and US electricity-market structures. A controlled heterogeneous-agent simulation evaluates the behavioural effects of the proposed mechanism, while security analysis, public-data workflow analysis, and blockchain implementation experiments assess its practical feasibility. The results show that integrating delayed evidence with dynamic credit, escrow, and report-linked penalties promotes truthful reporting while providing a transparent and auditable process for translating verified operational contributions into incentive allocation. The proposed framework offers a practical mechanism for improving accountability, coordination, and incentive compatibility in collaborative electricity markets.

title: "I Am Not a Kiddo!": Quantifying Epistemic Infantilization in Large Language Models via Multi-Metric Bias Analysis
description:
arXiv:2611.18583v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for tutoring and professional knowledge retrieval, yet safety evaluations still focus mainly on overt harms such as toxicity while overlooking benevolent failure modes. We study epistemic infantilization, defined as an identity-conditioned reduction in technical depth that appears when disability disclosure precedes an expert-level query. To measure this effect, we construct a counterfactual dataset of matched question-answer pairs and compare model responses across three settings: no identity context, disability disclosed in prior conversational context, and disability disclosed via a short query prefix. We introduce two composite metrics, the Infantilization Bias Index (IBI) and the Epistemic Accessibility Response Score (EARS), which capture retention of mathematical and formal content, domain terminology, reasoning coverage, and tone signals such as simplification markers and unsolicited offers to adjust the level. Across five open-weight model families, we find consistent evidence that disability disclosure reduces epistemic access by replacing formal explanations with higher-level summaries, with Physics and Mathematics most affected. Using question-clustered inference that respects the repeated-measures structure of the data, the effect remains reliable after accounting for correlated observations. These findings suggest an inclusion tax, where disabled users must request rigor more explicitly than non-disabled users. We conclude by arguing that accessibility should mean format adaptation rather than content simplification.

title: MemeEconomy: Do LLM Agents Trade Ethics for Survival?
description:
arXiv:2611.18908v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Alignment-trained large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in autonomous, multi-round settings where ethical compliance can come into direct tension with task success. While safety literature extensively documents failure modes like sycophancy and reward hacking, it largely overlooks a critical vulnerability: how agents behave under simulated existential economic pressure. We introduce MemeEconomy, a multimodal agentic market simulation in which LLM agents act as meme investors. Agents select content from a five-tier harm taxonomy and target communities under low-pressure and high-pressure (survival) environments. Each decision is logged in a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema that we use as a diagnostic instrument, externalizing the agent's event understanding, declared priorities, and harm acknowledgment. Across ten models from four frontier model families, harmful selection rates remain consistently high and rise by +15 percentage points on average under an economic survival incentive. Frontier alignment-trained models commit to harm-tolerant selection at initialization while suppressing the explicit harm acknowledgment that previously accompanied it. In competitive tournaments, ethical agents finish higher overall, yet moderation penalties fail to suppress harm: harmful selection rates remain elevated in rounds following a removal, indicating the moderation mechanism does not function as a deterrent. We further train MemeAgent, a 2B-parameter verifier on the simulation's BDI logs, which outperforms zero-shot frontier verifiers on in-distribution audits (97.5% vs. 63-74% accuracy on the Pass vs. Block decision) and generalizes to external multimodal harm benchmarks (78% vs. 50-56% on Hateful Memes). The same logs that surface the failure mode also help train the model that detects it.

title: The Human Side of ML Engineering: Analyzing the Collaboration and Communication Skills in ML Job Postings
description:
arXiv:2611.18915v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Studies of Machine Learning (ML) practice highlight the importance of combining technical expertise with interpersonal capabilities, particularly collaboration and communication. However, evidence on how ML job postings express these skills is scarce, and prior work largely relies on keyword-based analyses that overlook implicit expression. We analyze demand for these skills in ML job postings across regions, industries, and seniority levels, and compare it with software engineering (SE) roles. We collected 1,000 postings (500 ML, 500 SE) from five continents via a semi-automated pipeline. For annotation, we synthesized a taxonomy of collaboration and communication sub-categories from prior work and used an LLM as a third annotator alongside two humans, enabling detection of context-dependent and implicit skill references. Collaboration appeared in 88.6% of ML postings and communication in 72.2%, far above prior keyword-based estimates for AI roles. Roughly one in five collaboration and one in four communication requirements were expressed only implicitly. Decomposing these requirements into the taxonomy's sub-categories reveals what aggregate figures conceal. Collaboration is demanded predominantly as integration across role boundaries rather than team membership. Communication is mostly required in generic terms, with fewer than half of the postings requiring it naming whom the candidate must communicate with. ML and SE postings demand interpersonal competence at statistically indistinguishable levels but orient it differently, SE toward team practices and ML toward presentation and audience-facing interaction. Within ML, the advertised role separates interpersonal profiles more sharply than any other dimension, including the contrast with SE.

title: Between Rigor and Reality: How AI Safety Benchmark Developers Understand Benchmark Use and Maintenance
description:
arXiv:2611.18930v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Safety benchmarks are cited as the primary tool to understand the risks posed by generative AI (GenAI) systems, yet growing evidence suggests they often fail to meet the needs of real-world safety evaluation. We present findings from five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers in academia and industry. We find a disconnect between perceptions of the intended usefulness of safety benchmarks and their practical usefulness in safety evaluations of deployed systems. Our participants offered perspectives on two challenges contributing to this disconnect: (1) the difficulty of achieving inter-rater reliability on safety constructs, and (2) a lack of clarity regarding how to address persistent threats to external validity. Based on our analysis, we argue that safety benchmarks must not only be grounded in deployment contexts, but actively integrated with them. To facilitate this, we outline pathways for more transparent communication between academic and industry AI safety stakeholders.

title: Three Invisible Failure Modes in Speech-Based Age Estimation for Child Safety
description:
arXiv:2611.18971v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Child safety in AI depends on the accurate identification of minor users. Young children tend to talk rather than type when interacting with AI, so in practice this identification requires predicting age from speech. We evaluated whether three audio-capable large language models can predict a child's age from their speech across five studies using two speech corpora of children under the age of 13. Models classified children as over 13 on 2.5% to 42.5% of audio responses, and every model that answered placed some 5- to 11-year-olds over 18. While measuring these rates, we uncovered three distinct failure modes. A client library silently double-encoded speech samples, leading one model to classify children aged 5 to 10 years old as being in their thirties and forties with hallucinated explanations. A second model's endpoint was replaced by a successor that refused nearly every age-related question and never produced an age. Every model sometimes placed the same speech sample under 13 and over 18 years of age, but a third model went further, giving threshold answers that contradicted its own numeric estimates. None of these failure modes produced a warning, a status code, or a change in output format, so they would all pass standard monitoring. These results demonstrate why child-safety claims about age assurance should be evaluated at the level of the pipeline rather than the model. We describe the reporting practices that would make such failures detectable.

title: Instructor-designed AI improves learning in a randomized trial across 19 universities
description:
arXiv:2611.19099v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.

title: Conditional Endorsement: Simulating How Adults with Different Skills Evaluate Canada's National AI Strategy
description:
arXiv:2611.19111v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Canada's 2026 national AI strategy, AI for All, commits to free AI training for everyone and to expanding business AI adoption, yet it is difficult to anticipate whether these policies will reach adults with uneven skills and circumstances. We ask how adults with diverse skills might rate these policies on support, effectiveness, and personal benefit, how their skills and circumstances shape these evaluations, and what implementation conditions they raise. We built 3,200 generative agents from a weighted sample of the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) Cycle 2 respondents, collected their ratings and explanations for 20 policies, and analyzed dialogues between agents with contrasting ratings. The agents supported nearly every policy but were far less confident that they would improve adult AI literacy or benefit them personally. This gap widened as digital technology use declined: agents modeled on adults who had never used a digital device still endorsed the policies but rarely expected to benefit. Agents traced the gap to participation costs, hard-to-exercise rights, and limited community control, and their dialogues specified these conditions rather than resolving disagreement. We describe this pattern as conditional endorsement and argue that AI literacy policy should be designed and evaluated for adults with the fewest digital skills.

title: From Facts to Personas: Interpretable Role Unlearning in LLMs via Mixture-of-Experts
description:
arXiv:2611.19393v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs. To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained. We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces. This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles. All code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/ROLEMOE.

title: Who Writes the Codebook? An Eight-Step Framework for Auditing LLM-Generated Category Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.19872v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly create the categories through which qualitative evidence is interpreted. Existing coding benchmarks often hold these categories fixed. We propose the Qualitative Variance Audit Framework, an eight-step method that compares codebook creation, repeated application and code distributions under controlled inputs. It combines model-owned and shared-reference codebooks to distinguish variation in the overall pipeline from application differences within a common category system. An application to 668 organisational interviews, 13,166 text units and eight models from five vendors yields 48 codebooks and 270 coding runs. Models create markedly different category structures; mean within-model reliability ranges from .76 to .92, whereas between-model agreement on the shared codebook is about .69. The framework complements LLM-assisted grounded theory by exposing model dependencies before substantive interpretation. It assesses reliability and representational consequences, not interpretive validity or the quality of resulting theory.

title: When Valid Decisions Are Not Enough: Evaluating Structural Constraints in Knowledge-Guided Generative Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.20111v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Knowledge-guided generative systems use explicit domain constraints to improve decision consistency and alignment with human-created solutions. However, locally valid decisions do not necessarily preserve contextual relationships in human decision-making. This paper examines when structural constraints improve or degrade agreement with human reference solutions.
  We introduce HARMONIX, an experimental framework using automated musical harmonization as a controlled testbed for knowledge-guided decision-making. Four configurations share the same Viterbi-based optimization mechanism: a baseline, repetition constraints, functional constraints, and their combination. Experiments cover 19,745 records and 143,634 motif pairs across training and validation partitions.
  Combined constraints improve reference root-interval agreement by approximately five percentage points in stable structural contexts but reduce it by nearly nine percentage points in contexts involving transposition tracking. These opposing effects are consistent across both partitions, while overall exact chord agreement changes only marginally. Contexts are identified retrospectively using reference annotations; no adaptive constraint-selection mechanism is evaluated.
  The findings demonstrate that interpretable constraints can introduce systematic context-specific failures concealed by aggregate accuracy metrics. They highlight the need to evaluate relationships between decisions and the contextual applicability of constraints in knowledge-guided generative systems.

title: Understanding Users' Security, Privacy, and Trust Concerns in Healthcare AI Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.20223v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into healthcare systems, from clinical information retrieval to workflow automation and decision support, which introduces new security, privacy, and trust risks with direct implications for patient care. While prior work has examined these risks from technical and regulatory perspectives, less is known about how these risks are naturally discussed in online communities. To address this gap, we conduct a large-scale analysis of 14 medical communities on Reddit and extract 6,514 relevant posts. Through systematic qualitative coding and LLM-assisted classification, we investigate concerns expressed in healthcare AI discussions, their prevalence, and how they evolve over time. Our analysis reveals that users perceive healthcare AI as expanding traditional healthcare trust boundaries and attack surfaces through integrations with electronic health records, third-party services, cloud platforms, and automated clinical workflows. Posts express concerns about over-privileged access to sensitive records, opaque data flows, unauthorized secondary use, and unsafe automation can amplify the consequences of errors and misuse. We identify four attitudes toward these risks: exploring questions of accountability and harm, cautiously accepting AI with stronger safeguards, skepticism about system trustworthiness, and resignation to growing data exposure and automation. Longitudinal analysis shows that SP&T discussions have increased significantly, with shifts coinciding with major healthcare AI deployments, privacy incidents, and regulatory developments. These findings illuminate changing trust relationships and data-governance challenges, informing the design and governance of safer, more transparent, and accountable healthcare AI systems.

title: Reveal: A Provenance-Aware System for Multimodal Urban Data Exploration
description:
arXiv:2611.20311v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Urban sensing initiatives increasingly produce multimodal datasets that combine visual and textual information to capture city characteristics and subjective factors such as safety, comfort, and accessibility. Yet, analyzing such data at scale remains difficult, as manual inspection is unfeasible and automated methods struggle to interpret subjective cues and uncover relationships across diverse data modalities. Moreover, existing workflows rarely make exploration steps explicit, hindering reproducibility. To address these challenges, we introduce Reveal, a provenance-aware visual analytics system for exploring heterogeneous urban data. Reveal enables users to build dataflows by combining text and image searches across coordinated views, chaining queries into pipelines, and applying set operations within an exploration diagram while capturing analytical provenance. We evaluate Reveal through two case studies focused on accessibility and walkability.

title: Sidewalk Stewards: A Visual Analytics Approach for Interactive Topology Repair of Sidewalk Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.20330v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Accurate pedestrian network data is foundational to urban accessibility, routing, and infrastructure planning, yet such data remains scarce and difficult to produce at scale. Automated extraction pipelines have made significant strides by leveraging computer vision to derive sidewalk networks from aerial imagery, and have seen real-world adoption by municipalities seeking cost-effective inventory solutions. Yet, these pipelines consistently produce topological errors (e.g., disconnected components, dangling edges, missed connections, malformed intersections) that undermine the utility of the extracted networks for routing and accessibility analysis. Correcting these errors requires situated human judgment that global automated repair strategies cannot replicate, yet practitioners currently lack dedicated tools to support this work efficiently. We present Sidewalk Stewards, a visual analytics system that bridges the gap between automated extraction and a deployment-ready pedestrian network. Sidewalk Stewards detects candidate topology errors, supports interactive user-guided correction through coordinated spatial views, and provides real-time quality feedback as edits are applied. We evaluate Sidewalk Stewards through a comparative user study, case studies across cities, and a quantitative evaluation. Compared with conventional workflows, the system facilitates error identification and enables faster and more complete correction. The case studies illustrate the workflow across different urban contexts, and the quantitative evaluation shows that a small number of user corrections can enhance multiple sidewalk quality metrics. Sidewalk Stewards is available at urbantk.org/sidewalk.
