title: Toward Operationalizing Rasmussen in Evolving Software Systems
description:
arXiv:2602.05483v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Rasmussen's qualitative drift model explains how successive, locally successful adaptations under efficiency pressures can move a system toward unacceptable operation. Brooker and Hochstein applied this perspective conceptually to software operations without specifying a quantitative procedure for observing drift. We take a step in this direction and propose a runtime observer that quantitatively operationalizes the model's observable part for evolving software. The proposed observer is intended to give engineers evidence for pausing or revising adaptation before declared operating limits are crossed. It tracks how activity or resource use is distributed across components and types of work. Measurement history quantifies accumulated change and recent movement toward or away from current limits. Assuming that direction and limits remain unchanged, the proposed observer calculates the first constraint ahead and the amount of further change required to reach it. Measurements remain comparable across supported component changes, while policy revisions are distinguished from changes in execution. Preliminary runtime studies demonstrated these distinctions under annotated software changes and revised retry limits. A separate multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) experiment detected CPU redistribution earlier with log-ratio coordinates than with raw shares, motivating investigation of representation-dependent observation. Further work will ground constraints in service outcomes, investigate runtime-model acquisition, and test whether decisions informed by observed drift reduce violations at acceptable useful-work loss and intervention cost.

title: From Survey Histories to Interpretable Digital Twins: Auto-Discovering Task-Specific Personas and Behavioral Mechanisms
description:
arXiv:2608.20344v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: LLM-based "digital twins" aim to simulate how an individual would behave in new environments or respond to novel questions, given some representation of that individual's prior responses. We ask whether long survey histories can be transformed into compact, task-specific personas that remain predictive for unseen respondents and products within the same task while making simulated decisions more interpretable. We introduce an iterative auto-discovery pipeline that constructs persona representations and learns how persona evidence influences simulated responses. We evaluate the procedure on the 40-item Product Preferences--Pricing task of Twin-2K-500 (Toubia et al., 2025), learning from 20 respondents and 20 products and evaluating the frozen representation and mechanism on 30 unseen respondents and 20 unseen products. The holdout answers come from two survey waves, and every prediction is scored against each wave separately. For gpt-5.4-nano, replacing the full survey transcript with the learned channel representation and mechanism improves exact accuracy from 0.573 to 0.623 and from 0.558 to 0.626 in the two waves. Larger and cross-provider simulators (gpt-5.4, gpt-5-mini, qwen3-8b) using the full transcript do not achieve statistically significant improvements over the baseline in both waves, and none significantly outperforms the learned representation in either wave. This pattern shows that the learned representation produces consistent gains against human responses collected in both waves while retaining an explicit mapping from respondent evidence to predicted decisions.

title: ABHBench: Evaluating Moral Decision-Making of Foundation Models from an Agentic Perspective
description:
arXiv:2611.09326v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Foundation models are increasingly deployed as agentic systems that perceive context and act autonomously, raising the need to evaluate their moral behavior as active decision-makers. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ask models to judge human actions from third-person textual vignettes, leaving untested how models behave when they themselves become the acting agent. We introduce ABHBench, a multimodal benchmark built from Detroit: Become Human, an interactive narrative game, to evaluate how foundation models make moral decisions in first-person human-android dilemmas. ABHBench places foundation models in branching narrative scenarios with visual observations, dialogue, memory, and action choices. Inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, our framework measures Harmlessness, Obedience, and Self-preservation to capture the core tensions in human-AI relations, along with Autonomy, Stability, and Certainty to assess decision-making patterns. Across 12 foundation models, we find that moral behavior changes substantially under situated agentic context: 75% of models shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal DBH scenario, and reasoning-enhanced models show no monotonic gains in consistency or human-oriented behavior. These results highlight the necessity of evaluating moral behavior in situated agentic contexts rather than relying on third-person judgment alone.
